newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-HAS THE BUBBLE BURST IN JAPANESE GAME?.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HAS THE BUBBLE BURST IN JAPANESE GAME?.

text.p: Japan's soccer boom seems to be on the wane.
J-League teams are struggling to keep their foreign stars as the novelty of playing in Japan is wearing off despite the big money on offer.

The latest major name to leave Japan is Danish international Michael Laudrup who packed his bags and left his apartment before it was announced that he was joining Dutch former European Cup champions Ajax Amsterdam.
Laudrup often voiced his discontent with Kobe, who had promised to spend money on other top foreign players when he signed for them during the mid-season break last year.
Laudrup helped Kobe win promotion to the J-League in his first season but they have struggled this year, mostly without him after he suffered a knee injury early in the campaign.
Another foreign international to have left Japan is Brazilian attacking midfielder Manoel of Cerezo Osaka, who is returning home to play for his former club Botafogo.
J-League teams are finding it difficult to attract replacements of the same quality.
Arsenal's former England captain David Platt is the latest big overseas name to turn down the chance of a move to Japan after contract negotiations with the Urawa Red Diamonds broke down.

The gaps are being filled by less glamorous players, such as ex-Norwich captain Mark Bowen, an attacking midfielder under Ossie Ardiles at Shimizu, and his former team mate Ian Crook, who last week signed for Hiroshima.
It is all a far cry from 1993 when the J-League was launched on a tide of optimism with world stars such as England striker Gary Lineker and Brazil's Zico.

The one bright spot is the recent run of success enjoyed by the national team. Since they were knocked out of the Asian Cup as defending champions in December, Japan have put together an impressive run of results.
After their recent 3-0 defeat of Nepal in a World Cup Asian zone qualifier, Japan are now virtually certain to qualify for the final regional round.
The national side also won the recent Kirin Cup tournament in Japan after victories over Croatia and Turkey.
Much of the credit for Japan's recent success lies at the feet of the most famous of the country's home-grown players, Kazuyoshi Miura.

Kazu's return to form has coincided with the emergence of 20-year-old Hiratsuka midfielder Hidetoshi Nakata. Since impressing on his international debut in a friendly against South Korea in May, Nakata has become a regular feature in the centre of Japan's midfield.
The two players have earned the nickname "Kazu-Hide Hot Line".
Japan will be hoping they don't lose the connection before what fans hope will be qualification for the World Cup finals in France next year.
